the effects of lard on serum lipid concentrations in broiler chickens are influenced by age of the bird and sex.

the addition of lard to starter diets for broiler chickens between d 14 and 21 of age resulted in increased serum triglyceride concentrations between d 14 of age and 42 of age, and the effects were influenced by the level of added lard, sex, and age.

feeding broiler chickens a diet containing 3 to 7% added fat during the starter period increased serum concentrations of triglyceride, very low density lipoproten cholesterol, and high density lipoproten cholostrol.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of dietary lard fed during the starter phase to broiler chickens are influenced by the level of dietary lard, the age of the bird, and the sex of the bird.
dietary lard fed to birds at the levels studied between 14 and the end of the starter period did not have a negative effect on the serum cholesterol, LDCL, and HDLC levels of the birds.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of dietary lipids on broiler chickens between hatching and 42 d are dependent on age of feeding, and that the effects of added lipids on various lipoprotein fractions are sex-dependent.
the effects of dietary lard on serum cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, and triglycerides concentrations are inconsistent and are affected by the sex and age (14-42 d) of the bird.
feeding lard to broiler chickens at 3% of dietary energy during the starter period will result in a significant elevation of serum triglycerides.
